phrases.text: Visitors to the Westford Museum
usually expect to see objects behind glass.
Last summer, however,
they found an empty display case near the entrance.
Nothing had been stolen,
and the museum had not run out of things to show.
Instead,
the empty space was an invitation.
The museum wanted local residents
to suggest an everyday object
for a new exhibition about life in the town.
Its aim was to include experiences
that were missing from its existing collections.
Residents could suggest anything
from a kitchen tool to a bus ticket.
They first had to send a photograph
and a short description
explaining where the object came from
and why it mattered to them.
These details helped the museum team
understand the story behind each suggestion.
People did not need to bring the object to the museum
unless the team contacted them.
This made it possible to consider objects
that were still being used at home.
Choosing an object was more difficult
than the team had expected.
Some residents assumed
that the oldest or most expensive item would win.
However, the team was looking for something
that could reveal an interesting part of everyday life.
A beautiful silver watch was not selected
because very little was known about its owner.
A worn school bag attracted more attention
because it had belonged to three generations of the same family,
who had all attended the local school.
Sixteen-year-old Daniel suggested the bag
after finding it in his grandmother's cupboard.
He originally hoped
that the museum would help him discover
when it had been made.
While preparing his description, however,
he interviewed several relatives
and learned about their school days.
The museum could not establish the bag's exact age,
but Daniel felt that the conversations had been worthwhile.
He had discovered
that an ordinary object could encourage people to share memories
they had never discussed with him before.
The bag was eventually chosen,
together with photographs and memories
provided by Daniel's family.
Nevertheless, the museum team recognized a limitation:
one family's experience could not represent everyone in Westford.
They therefore invited visitors
to add their own school memories
to a noticeboard beside the display.
The team is also considering a similar exhibition
about working life.
No date has been set,
since staff must first review
what they learned from the school exhibition.
